[[File:Digaonalsternuhr.jpg|alt=Diagonal Star Clock (Middle Kingdom)|thumb]] '''Ancient Egyptian Star Clocks''' are {{ill|Star Clock|de|Sternuhr|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Star Clock|qq=}}s in {{ill|Ancient Egypt|de|Altes Ägypten|lt=Ancient Egypt|lt_de=Alten Ägypten|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ancient Egypt|qq=}}. They are part of {{ill|Egyptian Astronomy|de|Astronomie im Alten Ägypten|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptian Astronomy|qq=}}. They served for {{ill|astronomical|de|Astronomie|lt=Astronomical|lt_de=astronomischen|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/astronomical|qq=}} {{ill|Timekeeping|de|Zeitmessung|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Timekeeping|qq=}} during the night. The model of the diagonal star clock, attested for the first time in the {{ill|First Intermediate Period (Egypt)|de|Erste Zwischenzeit (Ägypten)|lt=First Intermediate Period|lt_de=ersten Zwischenzeit|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/First Intermediate Period (Egypt)|qq=}}, used for the {{ill|Decan Stars|de|Baktiu|lt=Decan Stars|lt_de=Dekansterne|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Decan Stars|qq=}}—in addition to the well‐known instrumentarium of the {{ill|heliacal|de|heliakisch|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/heliacal|qq=}} rising—as a timekeeping criterion the {{ill|acronychal|de|Akronychisch|1=Acronychic|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/acronychal|13=User:Immanuelle/Acronychic|qq=}} {{ill|Culmination (Astronomy)|de|Kulmination (Astronomie)|lt=Culmination|lt_de=Kulminationen|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Culmination (Astronomy)|qq=}} and acronychal {{ill|Star|de|Stern|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Star|qq=}} settings. The individual night hour determined in this way had a different length compared to that of the later Ramesside Star Clock. Moreover, in the diagonal star clock the decans, including their associated decan stars, served as the basis for calculation. The Ramesside Star Clock, by contrast, was based on hourly stars without explicit decan assignment. Additionally, a 13th night hour was introduced, which enabled more precise timekeeping. The acronychal criteria used in the diagonal star clocks were incorporated into the new system of hourly stars. However, the {{ill|Innovations|de|Innovationen|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Innovations|qq=}} of the Ramesside Star Clock ultimately could not prevail, since the extended division of hours—compared to the 12‑hour system of the diagonal star clock traditionally used up to {{ill|Egypt in the Greco-Roman Period|de|Ägypten in griechisch-römischer Zeit|lt=Egypt in the Greco-Roman Period|lt_de=griechisch-römische Zeit|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt in the Greco-Roman Period|qq=}}—lacked the necessary historical basis. Moreover, the Ramesside Star Clock was not compatible with the mythology of the {{ill|Amduat|de|Amduat|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amduat|qq=}}. == Diagonal Star Clocks == The term "diagonal star clock" refers to the concept from {{ill|Linear Algebra|de|lineare Algebra|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Linear Algebra|qq=}}, in which the {{ill|Main Diagonal|de|Hauptdiagonale|lt=Main-|lt_de=Haupt-|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Main Diagonal|qq=}} and {{ill|Secondary Diagonal|de|Nebendiagonale|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Secondary Diagonal|qq=}} denote imagined lines that run diagonally from the top left to the bottom right through the {{ill|Egyptian Calendar|de|Ägyptischer Kalender|lt=Egyptian calendar scheme|lt_de=ägyptische Kalenderschema|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptian Calendar|qq=}}, thereby illustrating the passage of the {{ill|Decan Star|de|Dekan-Stern|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Decan Star|qq=}}s through the respective weeks. {| class="wikitable" style="width: 100%; border: 2px solid gray; text-align: center;" |- {{Ägyptologie TblHighlight}} |colspan="13" align=center style="background:#FFE39B"|'''{{ill|Diagonal Star Clock EA47605|ja|Diagonalsternuhr EA47605|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Diagonal Star Clock EA47605|qq=}}: Idealized ancient Egyptian calendar (division of the decans for the respective decades)'''Sarah Symons: ''A Star’s Year: The Annual Cycle in the Ancient Egyptian Sky.'' University of Leicester, 2007, p. 3. |- {{Ägyptologie TblHighlight}} ! [[Peret (Ancient Egypt)|1. P 1]] || [[Achet|21. A 4]] || 11. A 4 || 1. A 4 || 21. A 3 || 11. A 3 || 1. A 3 || 21. A 2 || 11. A 2 || 1. A 2 || 21. A 1 || 11. A 1 || 1. A 1 |- | '''[[Chentet-cheret|13]]''' | [[Chentet-heret|12]] | [[Tepi-a chentet|11]] | [[Schespet|10]] | [[Weschati-Bekati|9]] | [[Weschati-Bekati|8]] | [[Temat-cheret|7]] | [[Temat-heret|6]] | [[Pehui-djat|5]] | [[Hat-djat|4]] | [[Cheri-cheped-Kenmut|3]] | [[Kenmet (Decan)|2]] | [[Tepi-a Kenmet|1]] |- | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 |- | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 |- | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 |- | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 |- | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 |- | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 |- | 20 | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 |- | 21 | 20 | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 |- | 22 | 21 | 20 | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 |- | 23 | 22 | 21 | 20 | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 |- | 24 | 23 | 22 | 21 | 20 | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 |- | 25 | 24 | 23 | 22 | 21 | 20 | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' |} === Discovery === [[File:Sarg_des_Nacht_2.jpg|alt=So-called box coffin of Nacht|thumb]] The {{ill|Egyptologist|de|Ägyptologe|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptologist|qq=}} {{ill|Ludwig Borchardt|de|Ludwig Borchardt|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ludwig Borchardt|qq=}} (1863–1938) was the first to analyze the methods of ancient Egyptian timekeeping based on the fragments and coffin fittings that were found. Early on, he noted that timekeeping in ancient Egypt was predominantly based on astronomical observations. More precise astronomical calculations led to improved interpretations and the ability to assign the indications of the {{ill|Diagonal Star Clock|de|Diagonalsternuhr|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Diagonal Star Clock|qq=}} to their period of origin. The earliest evidence in the form of decorations is attested in the Middle Kingdom. During this period, such decorations are typically found on the undersides of coffin lids. The oldest documented diagonal star clocks date from the {{ill|9th Dynasty|de|9. Dynastie|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/9th Dynasty|qq=}}. The diagonal star clock found on coffin lid No. 9 can be dated to the reign of {{ill|Mentuhotep II|de|Mentuhotep II.|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mentuhotep II|qq=}} in the {{ill|11th Dynasty|de|11. Dynastie|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/11th Dynasty|qq=}}. Mentions in the {{ill|Pyramid Texts|de|Pyramidentexte|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Pyramid Texts|qq=}} suggest that the use of diagonal star clocks was likely in practice even before the beginnings of the {{ill|Old Kingdom (Egypt)|de|Altes Reich (Ägypten)|lt=Old Kingdom|lt_de=Alten Reichs|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old Kingdom (Egypt)|qq=}}, although this cannot yet be substantiated. Recent studies have shown that in the Old Kingdom the decans were arranged according to their heliacal risings and oriented to the “{{ill|Classical Celestial Map (Ancient Egypt)|de|Klassisches Himmelsbild (Altes Ägypten)|lt=Classical Celestial Map|lt_de=klassischen Himmelsbild|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Classical Celestial Map (Ancient Egypt)|qq=}}”. In the Middle Kingdom, the culminating decans replaced the “rising decans”. This systematic re-evaluation resulted in a new sequence of the decan stars in the {{ill|Coffin Texts|de|Sargtexte|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Coffin Texts|qq=}}.Alexandra von Lieven: ''Grundriss des Laufes der Sterne.'' Copenhagen 2007, p. 43. === Locations and Attribution of the Data === The coffins with diagonal star clocks originate from {{ill|Asyut|de|Assiut|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Asyut|qq=}}, {{ill|Thebes (Egypt)|de|Theben (Ägypten)|lt=Thebes|lt_de=Theben|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Thebes (Egypt)|qq=}}, {{ill|Gebelein|de|Gebelein|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gebelein|qq=}} and {{ill|Aswan|de|Assuan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Aswan|qq=}}. No differences in their arrangements can be discerned. These circumstances led to the conclusion that the indications of the diagonal star clocks point to an idealized calendar. Other astronomical records with calendar references indicate the locations of {{ill|Memphis (Egypt)|de|Memphis (Ägypten)|lt=Memphis|lt_de=Memphis|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Memphis (Egypt)|qq=}} and {{ill|Heliopolis|de|Heliopolis|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Heliopolis|qq=}}, which is why the indications of the diagonal star clocks most likely are uniformly based on the {{ill|Geographic Latitude|de|Geographische Breite|lt=30th Latitude|lt_de=30. Breitengrad|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Geographic Latitude|qq=}}. In the oldest attestations of the Middle Kingdom, the heliacal rising of the star {{ill|Sirius|de|Sirius|lt=Sothis|lt_de=Sothis|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sirius|qq=}} is dated in the twelfth nocturnal hour as the 18th decan, which, when converted, corresponds to {{ill|Peret (Ancient Egypt)|de|Peret (Altes Ägypten)|1=Season of the Emergence|lt=Peret|2=de|3=Peret (Altes Ägypten)|4=ja|5=ペレト|6=zh|7=播種季|8=ru|9=Перет|10=uk|11=Перет|qq=draft|13=Season of the Emergence|14=es|15=Estación de la emergencia|16=fr|17=Peret|18=pl|19=Peret|20=ro|21=Peret|lt=21st Peret II|lt_de=21. Peret II|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Peret (Ancient Egypt)|13=User:Immanuelle/Season of the Emergence|qq=}}. The Sothis date confirms the content of the coffin texts, according to which the decan risings determined the respective hours. The later association of dating with culmination was demonstrably not applied at that time, as the calendar data would then no longer correspond to the actual risings.Siegfried Schott: ''Altägyptische Festdaten'' (= ''Akademie der Wissenschaften und der Literatur (Mainz, Germany).; Abhandlungen der Geistes- und Sozialwissenschaftlichen Klasse.''). Verlag der Akademie der Wissenschaften und der Literatur, Mainz / Wiesbaden 1950, p. 25. === Working Principle === [[File:Dendera.jpg|alt=The Zodiac Signs from Dendera|thumb]] {{ill|Otto Neugebauer|de|Otto Neugebauer|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Otto Neugebauer|qq=}}, {{ill|Richard Anthony Parker|de|Richard Anthony Parker|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Richard Anthony Parker|qq=}} and {{ill|Christian Leitz|de|Christian Leitz|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Christian Leitz|qq=}} demonstrated that the methods of decan star calculation during the Greco-Roman period did not correspond to those of the {{ill|Middle Kingdom (Egypt)|de|Mittleres Reich|lt=Middle Kingdom of Egypt|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle Kingdom (Egypt)|qq=}}. In the former case, the twelve {{ill|Zodiac Signs from Dendera|de|Dendera#Tierkreise von Dendera|lt=Zodiac Signs from Dendera|lt_de=Tierkreiszeichen aus Dendera|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zodiac Signs from Dendera|qq=}} that had already been introduced served as the basis, which is why the division of the 36 decans and their nocturnal hours was aligned with the {{ill|Ecliptic|de|Ekliptik|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ecliptic|qq=}}. In the Middle Kingdom, neither an understanding of the {{ill|Ecliptic|de|Ekliptik|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ecliptic|qq=}} nor the foundation of the twelve zodiac signs was present. Thus, the operating principle of the diagonal star clocks was based on a different foundation.Christian Leitz: ''Altägyptische Sternuhren.'' Leuven 1995, p. 74. In the illustrations and decorations of tombs, the ''life cycle'' of the deities and decan stars was recorded in calendrical form. Together with the instrument of the {{ill|Sundial|de|Schattenuhr|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sundial|qq=}}, the Egyptians divided the day into the ''twelve hours of the day'' and the ''twelve hours of the night'', with the length of the daytime hours depending on the sun’s position. The night hours were divided into {{ill|Equal Hours|de|Äquale Stunden|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Equal Hours|qq=}} time units that were adjusted in length according to the respective {{ill|Season|de|Jahreszeit|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Season|qq=}}. Thus, the night was divided into twelve equally long hourly segments, which, however, did not correspond to those of the following day.Christian Leitz: ''Altägyptische Sternuhren.'' Leuven 1995, p. 75. The decan stars always indicated the end of the respective hour; for example, the heliacal rising of {{ill|Sirius|de|Sirius|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sirius|qq=}} according to the classification of the diagonal star clocks always occurred at the end of the twelfth night hour, ideally as the 18th decanal star. Christian Leitz points to the contradictory assumptions of {{ill|Otto Neugebauer|de|Otto Neugebauer|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Otto Neugebauer|qq=}}, {{ill|Richard Anthony Parker|de|Richard Anthony Parker|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Richard Anthony Parker|qq=}} and {{ill|Christian Leitz|de|Christian Leitz|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Christian Leitz|qq=}}, who, contrary to their own definitions, equated each night hour of the diagonal star clocks with 10° of the {{ill|Ecliptic|de|Ekliptik|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ecliptic|qq=}}. The corresponding calculations in connection with the {{ill|Ecliptic|de|Ekliptik|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ecliptic|qq=}} are based on a non-existent foundation and are therefore incorrect.Christian Leitz: ''Altägyptische Sternuhren.'' Leuven 1995, p. 73. === Decan Stars === In {{ill|Egyptian astronomy|de|Ägyptische Astronomie|lt=Egyptian astronomy|lt_de=ägyptischen Astronomie|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptian astronomy|qq=}}, the year of the Egyptian calendar was divided into 36 weeks of ten days each. The missing five days formed the ''{{ill|small year|de|Heriu-renpet|lt=small year|lt_de=kleine Jahr|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/small year|qq=}}''. To the weeks were assigned {{ill|decan stars|de|Baktiu|lt=decan stars|lt_de=Dekan-Sterne|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/decan stars|qq=}}, which, with their heliacal rising at intervals of ten days, gave their names to the 36 weeks. === Division of the Sky === {{Infobox hieroglyphs two-columns |TITEL = Division of the Sky |NAME-ERWEITERT = {{ill|Middle Kingdom (Egypt)|de|Mittleres Reich|lt=Middle Kingdom of Egypt|lt=Middle Kingdom|lt_de=Mittleres Reich|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle Kingdom (Egypt)|qq=}} |NAME = N14:Z2-pt:N35
Sebau-en-pet
''Sb3w-n-pt''
''Stars of the Sky'' |NAME2-ERWEITERT = {{ill|New Kingdom|de|Neues Reich|lt=New Kingdom|lt_de=Neues Reich|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/New Kingdom|qq=}} |NAME2 = D58-G1-V31:X1-M17-G43 N14:Z2 |NAME2-ERKLÄRUNG = Sebau-baktiu

''Working Stars'' }} Between the first heliacally rising and the acronychal culminating decan star, which "marks the first hour of the night", lie twenty decan stars. The "decan stars of the sky" (sebau-en-pet) had fixed celestial positions. Eight decan stars were always located in the east and symbolize the "birth stars" (meset), nine decan stars represent the "dying stars" ({{ill|Duat|de|Duat|lt=Duat|lt_de=scheni-duat|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Duat|qq=}}) in the west, while twelve decan stars are positioned in the middle of the sky as "working decan stars" (Baktiu). === Underworld === In the underworld (realm of the dead), there were always seven "dead stars" (scha-tuat). The "dead stars" had no special functions, but rather "slept" together with the dead until the next reincarnation. == Ramesside Star Clocks == [[File:Lepsius-228-III-ramsèsVI-détail.jpg|alt=16. Achet I (Thoth) in the tomb of Ramses VI.|thumb]] The four extant examples from the tombs of Ramses VI, Ramses VII, and Ramses IX could be assembled into a largely complete version. A Ramesside Star Clock contains 24 panels, one each for the first and the 16th day of the month in the twelve‐month ancient Egyptian calendar year. Each panel is divided into 13 hour lines, which represent the period from sunset to sunrise. The first line symbolized ''the beginning of the night'', which began immediately after sunset. Lines two to 13 represented the respective end of the twelve night hours. Each individual ''hour line'' contains three entries: hour, star name, and positional indication. The listed stars either belonged to an ancient Egyptian constellation or represented individual stars. The Ramesside Star Clocks included a total of 47 different stars. The positional indications referred to the seven possible positions: ''right shoulder'', ''right ear'', ''right eye'', ''middle'', ''left eye'', ''left ear'' and ''left shoulder''. The position ''middle'' stood for the meridian; the other six indications referred to positions east and west of the meridian. === Dating of the Ramesside Star Clocks === [[File:Meridiano.svg|alt=The meridian is drawn as an orange circle.|thumb]] Based on the constellations described in the Ramesside Star Clocks, Egyptologists of the 19th century already recognized that the data must refer to a time between 1500 and 1450 BCE. Otto Neugebauer and Richard Anthony Parker, who confirmed this time period, attempted to assign the respective stars. After a thorough analysis, both Egyptologists concluded that an exact identification of the individual star positions—and thus a more precise dating—was not possible. Christian Leitz was the first Egyptologist to deal in detail with the statements of Otto Neugebauer and Richard-Anthony Parker regarding the Ramesside Star Clocks. His research findings demonstrate that some star assignments were incorrect and, therefore, a precise chronological framework could not be established. Since {{ill|Seba-en-Sah|de|Seba-en-Sah|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seba-en-Sah|qq=}}, the principal star of the ancient Egyptian constellation {{ill|Sah (constellation)|de|Sah (Sternbild)|lt=Sah|lt_de=Sah|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sah (constellation)|qq=}}, could eventually be identified with certainty—and since Seba-en-Sah is also depicted in the lid scenes of the tomb of {{ill|Senenmut|de|Senenmut|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senenmut|qq=}} ({{ill|TT353|de|TT353|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/TT353|qq=}})—a day-accurate assignment was possible. In the tomb of Senenmut it is recorded that Seba-en-Sah culminated at [[Midnight]] on {{ill|23. Achet III|de|Achet#Datierungen|lt=23rd Achet III|lt_de=23. Achet III|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/23. Achet III|qq=}}. The constellations mentioned in Senenmut’s tomb, as in other ancient Egyptian sources, refer to the observational site of the calendrical Sothis risings, namely Memphis. {{ill|Rolf Krauss|de|Rolf Krauss|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Rolf Krauss|qq=}}, who postulated the hypothesis of changing observational sites ({{ill|Axiom|de|Axiom|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Axiom|qq=}}),, on the other hand, rejects an identification of Seba-en-Sah with {{ill|Rigel|de|Rigel|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Rigel|qq=}}, because in his published analyses {{ill|Elephantine|de|Elephantine|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Elephantine|qq=}} is favored as the observational site. Accepting the equation of Seba-en-Sah with Rigel would render his concept invalid. In the Ramesside Star Clocks, which were created only about three centuries later, the unchanged data from Senenmut’s tomb reappear, although in the {{ill|Egyptian calendar|de|altägyptischen Kalender|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptian calendar|qq=}} the star positions had shifted by more than two months. Astronomical calculations showed that the midnight culmination of Seba-en-Sah in conjunction with the other stellar data can be reconciled with the ancient Egyptian calendar and the observational site Memphis only for the years 1463/1462 BCE. {| class="wikitable zebra" style="background:#FFFAF0; width: 98%; border: 2px solid gray; text-align: center;" |- {{Ägyptologie TblHighlight}} !colspan="4" style="background:#FFE39B"| Altägyptischer Kalender der Ramessidischen Sternuhren im Jahr 1463/1462 v. [[File:Digaonalsternuhr.jpg|alt=Diagonal Star Clock (Middle Kingdom)|thumb]] '''Ancient Egyptian Star Clocks''' are {{ill|Star Clock|de|Sternuhr|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Star Clock|qq=}}s in {{ill|Ancient Egypt|de|Altes Ägypten|lt=Ancient Egypt|lt_de=Alten Ägypten|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ancient Egypt|qq=}}. They are part of {{ill|Egyptian Astronomy|de|Astronomie im Alten Ägypten|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptian Astronomy|qq=}}. They served for {{ill|astronomical|de|Astronomie|lt=Astronomical|lt_de=astronomischen|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/astronomical|qq=}} {{ill|Timekeeping|de|Zeitmessung|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Timekeeping|qq=}} during the night. The model of the diagonal star clock, attested for the first time in the {{ill|First Intermediate Period (Egypt)|de|Erste Zwischenzeit|lt=First Intermediate Period|lt_de=ersten Zwischenzeit|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/First Intermediate Period (Egypt)|qq=}}, used for the {{ill|Decan Stars|de|Baktiu|lt=Decan Stars|lt_de=Dekansterne|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Decan Stars|qq=}}—in addition to the well‐known instrumentarium of the {{ill|heliacal|de|heliakisch|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/heliacal|qq=}} rising—as a timekeeping criterion the {{ill|acronychal|de|Akronychisch|1=Acronychic|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/acronychal|13=User:Immanuelle/Acronychic|qq=}} {{ill|Culmination (Astronomy)|de|Kulmination (Astronomie)|lt=Culmination|lt_de=Kulminationen|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Culmination (Astronomy)|qq=}} and acronychal {{ill|Star|de|Stern|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Star|qq=}} settings. The individual night hour determined in this way had a different length compared to that of the later Ramesside Star Clock. Moreover, in the diagonal star clock the decans, including their associated decan stars, served as the basis for calculation. The Ramesside Star Clock, by contrast, was based on hourly stars without explicit decan assignment. Additionally, a 13th night hour was introduced, which enabled more precise timekeeping. The acronychal criteria used in the diagonal star clocks were incorporated into the new system of hourly stars. However, the {{ill|Innovations|de|Innovationen|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Innovations|qq=}} of the Ramesside Star Clock ultimately could not prevail, since the extended division of hours—compared to the 12‑hour system of the diagonal star clock traditionally used up to {{ill|Egypt in the Greco-Roman Period|de|Ägypten in griechisch-römischer Zeit|lt=Egypt in the Greco-Roman Period|lt_de=griechisch-römische Zeit|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt in the Greco-Roman Period|qq=}}—lacked the necessary historical basis. Moreover, the Ramesside Star Clock was not compatible with the mythology of the {{ill|Amduat|de|Amduat|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amduat|qq=}}. == Diagonal Star Clocks == The term "diagonal star clock" refers to the concept from {{ill|Linear Algebra|de|lineare Algebra|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Linear Algebra|qq=}}, in which the {{ill|Main Diagonal|de|Hauptdiagonale|lt=Main-|lt_de=Haupt-|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Main Diagonal|qq=}} and {{ill|Secondary Diagonal|de|Nebendiagonale|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Secondary Diagonal|qq=}} denote imagined lines that run diagonally from the top left to the bottom right through the {{ill|Egyptian Calendar|de|Ägyptischer Kalender|lt=Egyptian calendar scheme|lt_de=ägyptische Kalenderschema|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptian Calendar|qq=}}, thereby illustrating the passage of the {{ill|Decan Star|de|Dekan-Stern|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Decan Star|qq=}}s through the respective weeks. {| class="wikitable" style="width: 100%; border: 2px solid gray; text-align: center;" |- {{Ägyptologie TblHighlight}} |colspan="13" align=center style="background:#FFE39B"|'''{{ill|Diagonal Star Clock EA47605|ja|Diagonalsternuhr EA47605|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Diagonal Star Clock EA47605|qq=}}: Idealized ancient Egyptian calendar (division of the decans for the respective decades)'''Sarah Symons: ''A Star’s Year: The Annual Cycle in the Ancient Egyptian Sky.'' University of Leicester, 2007, p. 3. |- {{Ägyptologie TblHighlight}} ! Early on, he noted that timekeeping in ancient Egypt was predominantly based on astronomical observations. More precise astronomical calculations led to improved interpretations and the ability to assign the indications of the {{ill|Diagonal Star Clock|de|Diagonalsternuhr|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Diagonal Star Clock|qq=}} to their period of origin. The earliest evidence in the form of decorations is attested in the Middle Kingdom. During this period, such decorations are typically found on the undersides of coffin lids. The oldest documented diagonal star clocks date from the {{ill|9th Dynasty|de|9. Dynastie|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/9th Dynasty|qq=}}. The diagonal star clock found on coffin lid No. 9 can be dated to the reign of {{ill|Mentuhotep II|de|Mentuhotep II.|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mentuhotep II|qq=}} in the {{ill|11th Dynasty|de|11. Dynastie|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/11th Dynasty|qq=}}. Mentions in the {{ill|Pyramid Texts|de|Pyramidentexte|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Pyramid Texts|qq=}} suggest that the use of diagonal star clocks was likely in practice even before the beginnings of the {{ill|Old Kingdom (Egypt)|de|Altes Reich (Ägypten)|lt=Old Kingdom|lt_de=Alten Reichs|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old Kingdom (Egypt)|qq=}}, although this cannot yet be substantiated. Recent studies have shown that in the Old Kingdom the decans were arranged according to their heliacal risings and oriented to the “{{ill|Classical Celestial Map (Ancient Egypt)|de|Klassisches Himmelsbild (Altes Ägypten)|lt=Classical Celestial Map|lt_de=klassischen Himmelsbild|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Classical Celestial Map (Ancient Egypt)|qq=}}”. In the Middle Kingdom, the culminating decans replaced the “rising decans”. This systematic re-evaluation resulted in a new sequence of the decan stars in the {{ill|Coffin Texts|de|Sargtexte|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Coffin Texts|qq=}}.Alexandra von Lieven: ''Grundriss des Laufes der Sterne.'' Copenhagen 2007, p. 43. === Locations and Attribution of the Data === The coffins with diagonal star clocks originate from {{ill|Asyut|de|Assiut|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Asyut|qq=}}, {{ill|Thebes (Egypt)|de|Theben (Ägypten)|lt=Thebes|lt_de=Theben|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Thebes (Egypt)|qq=}}, {{ill|Gebelein|de|Gebelein|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gebelein|qq=}} and {{ill|Aswan|de|Assuan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Aswan|qq=}}. No differences in their arrangements can be discerned. These circumstances led to the conclusion that the indications of the diagonal star clocks point to an idealized calendar. Other astronomical records with calendar references indicate the locations of {{ill|Memphis (Egypt)|de|Memphis (Ägypten)|lt=Memphis|lt_de=Memphis|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Memphis (Egypt)|qq=}} and {{ill|Heliopolis|de|Heliopolis|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Heliopolis|qq=}}, which is why the indications of the diagonal star clocks most likely are uniformly based on the {{ill|Geographic Latitude|de|Geographische Breite|lt=30th Latitude|lt_de=30. Breitengrad|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Geographic Latitude|qq=}}. In the oldest attestations of the Middle Kingdom, the heliacal rising of the star {{ill|Sirius|de|Sirius|lt=Sothis|lt_de=Sothis|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sirius|qq=}} is dated in the twelfth nocturnal hour as the 18th decan, which, when converted, corresponds to {{ill|Peret (Ancient Egypt)|de|Peret (Altes Ägypten)|1=Season of the Emergence|lt=Peret|2=de|3=Peret (Altes Ägypten)|4=ja|5=ペレト|6=zh|7=播種季|8=ru|9=Перет|10=uk|11=Перет|qq=draft|13=Season of the Emergence|14=es|15=Estación de la emergencia|16=fr|17=Peret|18=pl|19=Peret|20=ro|21=Peret|lt=21st Peret II|lt_de=21. Peret II|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Peret (Ancient Egypt)|13=User:Immanuelle/Season of the Emergence|qq=}}. The Sothis date confirms the content of the coffin texts, according to which the decan risings determined the respective hours. The later association of dating with culmination was demonstrably not applied at that time, as the calendar data would then no longer correspond to the actual risings.Siegfried Schott: ''Altägyptische Festdaten'' (= ''Akademie der Wissenschaften und der Literatur (Mainz, Germany).; Abhandlungen der Geistes- und Sozialwissenschaftlichen Klasse.''). Verlag der Akademie der Wissenschaften und der Literatur, Mainz / Wiesbaden 1950, p. 25. === Working Principle === [[File:Dendera.jpg|alt=The Zodiac Signs from Dendera|thumb]] {{ill|Otto Neugebauer|de|Otto Neugebauer|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Otto Neugebauer|qq=}}, {{ill|Richard Anthony Parker|de|Richard Anthony Parker|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Richard Anthony Parker|qq=}} and {{ill|Christian Leitz|de|Christian Leitz|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Christian Leitz|qq=}} demonstrated that the methods of decan star calculation during the Greco-Roman period did not correspond to those of the {{ill|Middle Kingdom (Egypt)|de|Mittleres Reich|lt=Middle Kingdom of Egypt|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle Kingdom (Egypt)|qq=}}. In the former case, the twelve {{ill|Zodiac Signs from Dendera|de|Dendera#Tierkreise von Dendera|lt=Zodiac Signs from Dendera|lt_de=Tierkreiszeichen aus Dendera|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zodiac Signs from Dendera|qq=}} that had already been introduced served as the basis, which is why the division of the 36 decans and their nocturnal hours was aligned with the {{ill|Ecliptic|de|Ekliptik|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ecliptic|qq=}}. In the Middle Kingdom, neither an understanding of the {{ill|Ecliptic|de|Ekliptik|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ecliptic|qq=}} nor the foundation of the twelve zodiac signs was present. Thus, the operating principle of the diagonal star clocks was based on a different foundation.Christian Leitz: ''Altägyptische Sternuhren.'' Leuven 1995, p. 74. In the illustrations and decorations of tombs, the ''life cycle'' of the deities and decan stars was recorded in calendrical form. Together with the instrument of the {{ill|Sundial|de|Schattenuhr|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sundial|qq=}}, the Egyptians divided the day into the ''twelve hours of the day'' and the ''twelve hours of the night'', with the length of the daytime hours depending on the sun’s position. The night hours were divided into {{ill|Equal Hours|de|Äquale Stunden|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Equal Hours|qq=}} time units that were adjusted in length according to the respective {{ill|Season|de|Jahreszeit|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Season|qq=}}. Thus, the night was divided into twelve equally long hourly segments, which, however, did not correspond to those of the following day.Christian Leitz: ''Altägyptische Sternuhren.'' Leuven 1995, p. 75. The decan stars always indicated the end of the respective hour; for example, the heliacal rising of {{ill|Sirius|de|Sirius|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sirius|qq=}} according to the classification of the diagonal star clocks always occurred at the end of the twelfth night hour, ideally as the 18th decanal star. Christian Leitz points to the contradictory assumptions of {{ill|Otto Neugebauer|de|Otto Neugebauer|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Otto Neugebauer|qq=}}, {{ill|Richard Anthony Parker|de|Richard Anthony Parker|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Richard Anthony Parker|qq=}} and {{ill|Christian Leitz|de|Christian Leitz|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Christian Leitz|qq=}}, who, contrary to their own definitions, equated each night hour of the diagonal star clocks with 10° of the {{ill|Ecliptic|de|Ekliptik|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ecliptic|qq=}}. The corresponding calculations in connection with the {{ill|Ecliptic|de|Ekliptik|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ecliptic|qq=}} are based on a non-existent foundation and are therefore incorrect.Christian Leitz: ''Altägyptische Sternuhren.'' Leuven 1995, p. 73. === Decan Stars === In {{ill|Egyptian astronomy|de|Ägyptische Astronomie|lt=Egyptian astronomy|lt_de=ägyptischen Astronomie|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptian astronomy|qq=}}, the year of the Egyptian calendar was divided into 36 weeks of ten days each. The missing five days formed the ''{{ill|small year|de|Heriu-renpet|lt=small year|lt_de=kleine Jahr|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/small year|qq=}}''. To the weeks were assigned {{ill|decan stars|de|Baktiu|lt=decan stars|lt_de=Dekan-Sterne|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/decan stars|qq=}}, which, with their heliacal rising at intervals of ten days, gave their names to the 36 weeks. === Division of the Sky === {{Infobox hieroglyphs two-columns |TITEL = Division of the Sky |NAME-ERWEITERT = {{ill|Middle Kingdom (Egypt)|de|Mittleres Reich|lt=Middle Kingdom of Egypt|lt=Middle Kingdom|lt_de=Mittleres Reich|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle Kingdom (Egypt)|qq=}} |NAME = N14:Z2-pt:N35
Sebau-en-pet
''Sb3w-n-pt''
''Stars of the Sky'' |NAME2-ERWEITERT = {{ill|New Kingdom|de|Neues Reich|lt=New Kingdom|lt_de=Neues Reich|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/New Kingdom|qq=}} |NAME2 = D58-G1-V31:X1-M17-G43 N14:Z2 |NAME2-ERKLÄRUNG = Sebau-baktiu
''Sb3w-b3k.tjw''
''Working Stars'' }} Between the first heliacally rising and the acronychal culminating decan star, which "marks the first hour of the night", lie twenty decan stars. The "decan stars of the sky" (sebau-en-pet) had fixed celestial positions. Eight decan stars were always located in the east and symbolize the "birth stars" (meset), nine decan stars represent the "dying stars" ({{ill|Duat|de|Duat|lt=Duat|lt_de=scheni-duat|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Duat|qq=}}) in the west, while twelve decan stars are positioned in the middle of the sky as "working decan stars" (Baktiu). === Underworld === In the underworld (realm of the dead), there were always seven "dead stars" (scha-tuat). The "dead stars" had no special functions, but rather "slept" together with the dead until the next reincarnation. == Ramesside Star Clocks == [[File:Lepsius-228-III-ramsèsVI-détail.jpg|alt=16. Achet I (Thoth) in the tomb of Ramses VI.|thumb]] The four extant examples from the tombs of Ramses VI, Ramses VII, and Ramses IX could be assembled into a largely complete version. A Ramesside Star Clock contains 24 panels, one each for the first and the 16th day of the month in the twelve‐month ancient Egyptian calendar year. Each panel is divided into 13 hour lines, which represent the period from sunset to sunrise. The first line symbolized ''the beginning of the night'', which began immediately after sunset. Lines two to 13 represented the respective end of the twelve night hours. Each individual ''hour line'' contains three entries: hour, star name, and positional indication. The listed stars either belonged to an ancient Egyptian constellation or represented individual stars. The Ramesside Star Clocks included a total of 47 different stars. The positional indications referred to the seven possible positions: ''right shoulder'', ''right ear'', ''right eye'', ''middle'', ''left eye'', ''left ear'' and ''left shoulder''. The position ''middle'' stood for the meridian; the other six indications referred to positions east and west of the meridian. === Dating of the Ramesside Star Clocks === [[File:Meridiano.svg|alt=The meridian is drawn as an orange circle.|thumb]] Based on the constellations described in the Ramesside Star Clocks, Egyptologists of the 19th century already recognized that the data must refer to a time between 1500 and 1450 BCE. Otto Neugebauer and Richard Anthony Parker, who confirmed this time period, attempted to assign the respective stars. After a thorough analysis, both Egyptologists concluded that an exact identification of the individual star positions—and thus a more precise dating—was not possible. Christian Leitz was the first Egyptologist to deal in detail with the statements of Otto Neugebauer and Richard-Anthony Parker regarding the Ramesside Star Clocks. His research findings demonstrate that some star assignments were incorrect and, therefore, a precise chronological framework could not be established. Since {{ill|Seba-en-Sah|de|Seba-en-Sah|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seba-en-Sah|qq=}}, the principal star of the ancient Egyptian constellation {{ill|Sah (constellation)|de|Sah (Sternbild)|lt=Sah|lt_de=Sah|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sah (constellation)|qq=}}, could eventually be identified with certainty—and since Seba-en-Sah is also depicted in the lid scenes of the tomb of {{ill|Senenmut|de|Senenmut|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senenmut|qq=}} ({{ill|TT353|de|TT353|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/TT353|qq=}})—a day-accurate assignment was possible. In the tomb of Senenmut it is recorded that Seba-en-Sah culminated at [[Midnight]] on {{ill|23. Achet III|de|Achet#Datierungen|lt=23rd Achet III|lt_de=23. Achet III|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/23. Achet III|qq=}}. The constellations mentioned in Senenmut’s tomb, as in other ancient Egyptian sources, refer to the observational site of the calendrical Sothis risings, namely Memphis. {{ill|Rolf Krauss|de|Rolf Krauss|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Rolf Krauss|qq=}}, who postulated the hypothesis of changing observational sites ({{ill|Axiom|de|Axiom|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Axiom|qq=}}),, on the other hand, rejects an identification of Seba-en-Sah with {{ill|Rigel|de|Rigel|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Rigel|qq=}}, because in his published analyses {{ill|Elephantine|de|Elephantine|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Elephantine|qq=}} is favored as the observational site. Accepting the equation of Seba-en-Sah with Rigel would render his concept invalid. In the Ramesside Star Clocks, which were created only about three centuries later, the unchanged data from Senenmut’s tomb reappear, although in the {{ill|Egyptian calendar|de|altägyptischen Kalender|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptian calendar|qq=}} the star positions had shifted by more than two months. Astronomical calculations showed that the midnight culmination of Seba-en-Sah in conjunction with the other stellar data can be reconciled with the ancient Egyptian calendar and the observational site Memphis only for the years 1463/1462 BCE. {| class="wikitable zebra" style="background:#FFFAF0; width: 98%; border: 2px solid gray; text-align: center;" |- {{Ägyptologie TblHighlight}} !colspan="4" style="background:#FFE39B"| Altägyptischer Kalender der Ramessidischen Sternuhren im Jahr 1463/1462 v. [[File:Digaonalsternuhr.jpg|alt=Diagonal Star Clock (Middle Kingdom)|thumb]] '''Ancient Egyptian Star Clocks''' are {{ill|Star Clock|de|Sternuhr|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Star Clock|qq=}}s in {{ill|Ancient Egypt|de|Altes Ägypten|lt=Ancient Egypt|lt_de=Alten Ägypten|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ancient Egypt|qq=}}. They are part of {{ill|Egyptian Astronomy|de|Astronomie im Alten Ägypten|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptian Astronomy|qq=}}. They served for {{ill|astronomical|de|Astronomie|lt=Astronomical|lt_de=astronomischen|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/astronomical|qq=}} {{ill|Timekeeping|de|Zeitmessung|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Timekeeping|qq=}} during the night. The model of the diagonal star clock, attested for the first time in the {{ill|First Intermediate Period (Egypt)|de|Erste Zwischenzeit|lt=First Intermediate Period|lt_de=ersten Zwischenzeit|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/First Intermediate Period (Egypt)|qq=}}, used for the {{ill|Decan Stars|de|Baktiu|lt=Decan Stars|lt_de=Dekansterne|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Decan Stars|qq=}}—in addition to the well‐known instrumentarium of the {{ill|heliacal|de|heliakisch|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/heliacal|qq=}} rising—as a timekeeping criterion the {{ill|acronychal|de|Akronychisch|1=Acronychic|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/acronychal|13=User:Immanuelle/Acronychic|qq=}} {{ill|Culmination (Astronomy)|de|Kulmination (Astronomie)|lt=Culmination|lt_de=Kulminationen|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Culmination (Astronomy)|qq=}} and acronychal {{ill|Star|de|Stern|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Star|qq=}} settings. The individual night hour determined in this way had a different length compared to that of the later Ramesside Star Clock. Moreover, in the diagonal star clock the decans, including their associated decan stars, served as the basis for calculation. The Ramesside Star Clock, by contrast, was based on hourly stars without explicit decan assignment. Additionally, a 13th night hour was introduced, which enabled more precise timekeeping. The acronychal criteria used in the diagonal star clocks were incorporated into the new system of hourly stars. However, the {{ill|Innovations|de|Innovationen|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Innovations|qq=}} of the Ramesside Star Clock ultimately could not prevail, since the extended division of hours—compared to the 12‑hour system of the diagonal star clock traditionally used up to {{ill|Egypt in the Greco-Roman Period|de|Ägypten in griechisch-römischer Zeit|lt=Egypt in the Greco-Roman Period|lt_de=griechisch-römische Zeit|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egypt in the Greco-Roman Period|qq=}}—lacked the necessary historical basis. Moreover, the Ramesside Star Clock was not compatible with the mythology of the {{ill|Amduat|de|Amduat|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amduat|qq=}}. == Diagonal Star Clocks == The term "diagonal star clock" refers to the concept from {{ill|Linear Algebra|de|lineare Algebra|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Linear Algebra|qq=}}, in which the {{ill|Main Diagonal|de|Hauptdiagonale|lt=Main-|lt_de=Haupt-|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Main Diagonal|qq=}} and {{ill|Secondary Diagonal|de|Nebendiagonale|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Secondary Diagonal|qq=}} denote imagined lines that run diagonally from the top left to the bottom right through the {{ill|Egyptian Calendar|de|Ägyptischer Kalender|lt=Egyptian calendar scheme|lt_de=ägyptische Kalenderschema|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptian Calendar|qq=}}, thereby illustrating the passage of the {{ill|Decan Star|de|Dekan-Stern|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Decan Star|qq=}}s through the respective weeks. {| class="wikitable" style="width: 100%; border: 2px solid gray; text-align: center;" |- {{Ägyptologie TblHighlight}} |colspan="13" align=center style="background:#FFE39B"|'''{{ill|Diagonal Star Clock EA47605|ja|Diagonalsternuhr EA47605|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Diagonal Star Clock EA47605|qq=}}: Idealized ancient Egyptian calendar (division of the decans for the respective decades)'''Sarah Symons: ''A Star’s Year: The Annual Cycle in the Ancient Egyptian Sky.'' University of Leicester, 2007, p. 3. |- {{Ägyptologie TblHighlight}} ! [[Peret (Ancient Egypt)|1. P 1]] || [[Achet|21. A 4]] || 11. A 4 || 1. A 4 || 21. A 3 || 11. A 3 || 1. A 3 || 21. A 2 || 11. A 2 || 1. A 2 || 21. A 1 || 11. A 1 || 1. A 1 |- | '''[[Chentet-cheret|13]]''' | [[Chentet-heret|12]] | [[Tepi-a chentet|11]] | [[Schespet|10]] | [[Weschati-Bekati|9]] | [[Weschati-Bekati|8]] | [[Temat-cheret|7]] | [[Temat-heret|6]] | [[Pehui-djat|5]] | [[Hat-djat|4]] | [[Cheri-cheped-Kenmut|3]] | [[Kenmet (Decan)|2]] | [[Tepi-a Kenmet|1]] |- | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 |- | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 |- | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 |- | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 |- | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 |- | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 |- | 20 | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 |- | 21 | 20 | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 |- | 22 | 21 | 20 | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 | 10 |- | 23 | 22 | 21 | 20 | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 | 11 |- | 24 | 23 | 22 | 21 | 20 | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' | 12 |- | 25 | 24 | 23 | 22 | 21 | 20 | 19 | 18 | 17 | 16 | 15 | 14 | '''13''' |} === Discovery === [[File:Sarg_des_Nacht_2.jpg|alt=So-called box coffin of Nacht|thumb]] The {{ill|Egyptologist|de|Ägyptologe|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptologist|qq=}} {{ill|Ludwig Borchardt|de|Ludwig Borchardt|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ludwig Borchardt|qq=}} (1863–1938) was the first to analyze the methods of ancient Egyptian timekeeping based on the fragments and coffin fittings that were found. Early on, he noted that timekeeping in ancient Egypt was predominantly based on astronomical observations. More precise astronomical calculations led to improved interpretations and the ability to assign the indications of the {{ill|Diagonal Star Clock|de|Diagonalsternuhr|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Diagonal Star Clock|qq=}} to their period of origin. The earliest evidence in the form of decorations is attested in the Middle Kingdom. During this period, such decorations are typically found on the undersides of coffin lids. The oldest documented diagonal star clocks date from the {{ill|9th Dynasty|de|9. Dynastie|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/9th Dynasty|qq=}}. The diagonal star clock found on coffin lid No. 9 can be dated to the reign of {{ill|Mentuhotep II|de|Mentuhotep II.|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mentuhotep II|qq=}} in the {{ill|11th Dynasty|de|11. Dynastie|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/11th Dynasty|qq=}}. Mentions in the {{ill|Pyramid Texts|de|Pyramidentexte|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Pyramid Texts|qq=}} suggest that the use of diagonal star clocks was likely in practice even before the beginnings of the {{ill|Old Kingdom (Egypt)|de|Altes Reich (Ägypten)|lt=Old Kingdom|lt_de=Alten Reichs|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Old Kingdom (Egypt)|qq=}}, although this cannot yet be substantiated. Recent studies have shown that in the Old Kingdom the decans were arranged according to their heliacal risings and oriented to the “{{ill|Classical Celestial Map (Ancient Egypt)|de|Klassisches Himmelsbild (Altes Ägypten)|lt=Classical Celestial Map|lt_de=klassischen Himmelsbild|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Classical Celestial Map (Ancient Egypt)|qq=}}”. In the Middle Kingdom, the culminating decans replaced the “rising decans”. This systematic re-evaluation resulted in a new sequence of the decan stars in the {{ill|Coffin Texts|de|Sargtexte|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Coffin Texts|qq=}}.Alexandra von Lieven: ''Grundriss des Laufes der Sterne.'' Copenhagen 2007, p. 43. === Locations and Attribution of the Data === The coffins with diagonal star clocks originate from {{ill|Asyut|de|Assiut|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Asyut|qq=}}, {{ill|Thebes (Egypt)|de|Theben (Ägypten)|lt=Thebes|lt_de=Theben|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Thebes (Egypt)|qq=}}, {{ill|Gebelein|de|Gebelein|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gebelein|qq=}} and {{ill|Aswan|de|Assuan|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Aswan|qq=}}. No differences in their arrangements can be discerned. These circumstances led to the conclusion that the indications of the diagonal star clocks point to an idealized calendar. Other astronomical records with calendar references indicate the locations of {{ill|Memphis (Egypt)|de|Memphis (Ägypten)|lt=Memphis|lt_de=Memphis|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Memphis (Egypt)|qq=}} and {{ill|Heliopolis|de|Heliopolis|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Heliopolis|qq=}}, which is why the indications of the diagonal star clocks most likely are uniformly based on the {{ill|Geographic Latitude|de|Geographische Breite|lt=30th Latitude|lt_de=30. Breitengrad|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Geographic Latitude|qq=}}. In the oldest attestations of the Middle Kingdom, the heliacal rising of the star {{ill|Sirius|de|Sirius|lt=Sothis|lt_de=Sothis|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sirius|qq=}} is dated in the twelfth nocturnal hour as the 18th decan, which, when converted, corresponds to {{ill|Peret (Ancient Egypt)|de|Peret (Altes Ägypten)|1=Season of the Emergence|lt=Peret|2=de|3=Peret (Altes Ägypten)|4=ja|5=ペレト|6=zh|7=播種季|8=ru|9=Перет|10=uk|11=Перет|qq=draft|13=Season of the Emergence|14=es|15=Estación de la emergencia|16=fr|17=Peret|18=pl|19=Peret|20=ro|21=Peret|lt=21st Peret II|lt_de=21. Peret II|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Peret (Ancient Egypt)|13=User:Immanuelle/Season of the Emergence|qq=}}. The Sothis date confirms the content of the coffin texts, according to which the decan risings determined the respective hours. The later association of dating with culmination was demonstrably not applied at that time, as the calendar data would then no longer correspond to the actual risings.Siegfried Schott: ''Altägyptische Festdaten'' (= ''Akademie der Wissenschaften und der Literatur (Mainz, Germany).; Abhandlungen der Geistes- und Sozialwissenschaftlichen Klasse.''). Verlag der Akademie der Wissenschaften und der Literatur, Mainz / Wiesbaden 1950, p. 25. === Working Principle === [[File:Dendera.jpg|alt=The Zodiac Signs from Dendera|thumb]] {{ill|Otto Neugebauer|de|Otto Neugebauer|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Otto Neugebauer|qq=}}, {{ill|Richard Anthony Parker|de|Richard Anthony Parker|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Richard Anthony Parker|qq=}} and {{ill|Christian Leitz|de|Christian Leitz|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Christian Leitz|qq=}} demonstrated that the methods of decan star calculation during the Greco-Roman period did not correspond to those of the {{ill|Middle Kingdom (Egypt)|de|Mittleres Reich|lt=Middle Kingdom of Egypt|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle Kingdom (Egypt)|qq=}}. In the former case, the twelve {{ill|Zodiac Signs from Dendera|de|Dendera#Tierkreise von Dendera|lt=Zodiac Signs from Dendera|lt_de=Tierkreiszeichen aus Dendera|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zodiac Signs from Dendera|qq=}} that had already been introduced served as the basis, which is why the division of the 36 decans and their nocturnal hours was aligned with the {{ill|Ecliptic|de|Ekliptik|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ecliptic|qq=}}. In the Middle Kingdom, neither an understanding of the {{ill|Ecliptic|de|Ekliptik|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ecliptic|qq=}} nor the foundation of the twelve zodiac signs was present. Thus, the operating principle of the diagonal star clocks was based on a different foundation.Christian Leitz: ''Altägyptische Sternuhren.'' Leuven 1995, p. 74. In the illustrations and decorations of tombs, the ''life cycle'' of the deities and decan stars was recorded in calendrical form. Together with the instrument of the {{ill|Sundial|de|Schattenuhr|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sundial|qq=}}, the Egyptians divided the day into the ''twelve hours of the day'' and the ''twelve hours of the night'', with the length of the daytime hours depending on the sun’s position. The night hours were divided into {{ill|Equal Hours|de|Äquale Stunden|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Equal Hours|qq=}} time units that were adjusted in length according to the respective {{ill|Season|de|Jahreszeit|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Season|qq=}}. Thus, the night was divided into twelve equally long hourly segments, which, however, did not correspond to those of the following day.Christian Leitz: ''Altägyptische Sternuhren.'' Leuven 1995, p. 75. The decan stars always indicated the end of the respective hour; for example, the heliacal rising of {{ill|Sirius|de|Sirius|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sirius|qq=}} according to the classification of the diagonal star clocks always occurred at the end of the twelfth night hour, ideally as the 18th decanal star. Christian Leitz points to the contradictory assumptions of {{ill|Otto Neugebauer|de|Otto Neugebauer|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Otto Neugebauer|qq=}}, {{ill|Richard Anthony Parker|de|Richard Anthony Parker|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Richard Anthony Parker|qq=}} and {{ill|Christian Leitz|de|Christian Leitz|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Christian Leitz|qq=}}, who, contrary to their own definitions, equated each night hour of the diagonal star clocks with 10° of the {{ill|Ecliptic|de|Ekliptik|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ecliptic|qq=}}. The corresponding calculations in connection with the {{ill|Ecliptic|de|Ekliptik|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ecliptic|qq=}} are based on a non-existent foundation and are therefore incorrect.Christian Leitz: ''Altägyptische Sternuhren.'' Leuven 1995, p. 73. === Decan Stars === In {{ill|Egyptian astronomy|de|Ägyptische Astronomie|lt=Egyptian astronomy|lt_de=ägyptischen Astronomie|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptian astronomy|qq=}}, the year of the Egyptian calendar was divided into 36 weeks of ten days each. The missing five days formed the ''{{ill|small year|de|Heriu-renpet|lt=small year|lt_de=kleine Jahr|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/small year|qq=}}''. To the weeks were assigned {{ill|decan stars|de|Baktiu|lt=decan stars|lt_de=Dekan-Sterne|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/decan stars|qq=}}, which, with their heliacal rising at intervals of ten days, gave their names to the 36 weeks. === Division of the Sky === {{Infobox hieroglyphs two-columns |TITEL = Division of the Sky |NAME-ERWEITERT = {{ill|Middle Kingdom (Egypt)|de|Mittleres Reich|lt=Middle Kingdom of Egypt|lt=Middle Kingdom|lt_de=Mittleres Reich|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Middle Kingdom (Egypt)|qq=}} |NAME = N14:Z2-pt:N35
Sebau-en-pet
''Sb3w-n-pt''
''Stars of the Sky'' |NAME2-ERWEITERT = {{ill|New Kingdom|de|Neues Reich|lt=New Kingdom|lt_de=Neues Reich|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/New Kingdom|qq=}} |NAME2 = D58-G1-V31:X1-M17-G43 N14:Z2 |NAME2-ERKLÄRUNG = Sebau-baktiu
''Sb3w-b3k.tjw''
''Working Stars'' }} Between the first heliacally rising and the acronychal culminating decan star, which "marks the first hour of the night", lie twenty decan stars. The "decan stars of the sky" (sebau-en-pet) had fixed celestial positions. Eight decan stars were always located in the east and symbolize the "birth stars" (meset), nine decan stars represent the "dying stars" ({{ill|Duat|de|Duat|lt=Duat|lt_de=scheni-duat|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Duat|qq=}}) in the west, while twelve decan stars are positioned in the middle of the sky as "working decan stars" (Baktiu). === Underworld === In the underworld (realm of the dead), there were always seven "dead stars" (scha-tuat). The "dead stars" had no special functions, but rather "slept" together with the dead until the next reincarnation. == Ramesside Star Clocks == [[File:Lepsius-228-III-ramsèsVI-détail.jpg|alt=16. Achet I (Thoth) in the tomb of Ramses VI.|thumb]] The four extant examples from the tombs of Ramses VI, Ramses VII, and Ramses IX could be assembled into a largely complete version. A Ramesside Star Clock contains 24 panels, one each for the first and the 16th day of the month in the twelve‐month ancient Egyptian calendar year. Each panel is divided into 13 hour lines, which represent the period from sunset to sunrise. The first line symbolized ''the beginning of the night'', which began immediately after sunset. Lines two to 13 represented the respective end of the twelve night hours. Each individual ''hour line'' contains three entries: hour, star name, and positional indication. The listed stars either belonged to an ancient Egyptian constellation or represented individual stars. The Ramesside Star Clocks included a total of 47 different stars. The positional indications referred to the seven possible positions: ''right shoulder'', ''right ear'', ''right eye'', ''middle'', ''left eye'', ''left ear'' and ''left shoulder''. The position ''middle'' stood for the meridian; the other six indications referred to positions east and west of the meridian. === Dating of the Ramesside Star Clocks === [[File:Meridiano.svg|alt=The meridian is drawn as an orange circle.|thumb]] Based on the constellations described in the Ramesside Star Clocks, Egyptologists of the 19th century already recognized that the data must refer to a time between 1500 and 1450 BCE. Otto Neugebauer and Richard Anthony Parker, who confirmed this time period, attempted to assign the respective stars. After a thorough analysis, both Egyptologists concluded that an exact identification of the individual star positions—and thus a more precise dating—was not possible. Christian Leitz was the first Egyptologist to deal in detail with the statements of Otto Neugebauer and Richard-Anthony Parker regarding the Ramesside Star Clocks. His research findings demonstrate that some star assignments were incorrect and, therefore, a precise chronological framework could not be established. Since {{ill|Seba-en-Sah|de|Seba-en-Sah|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Seba-en-Sah|qq=}}, the principal star of the ancient Egyptian constellation {{ill|Sah (constellation)|de|Sah (Sternbild)|lt=Sah|lt_de=Sah|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sah (constellation)|qq=}}, could eventually be identified with certainty—and since Seba-en-Sah is also depicted in the lid scenes of the tomb of {{ill|Senenmut|de|Senenmut|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senenmut|qq=}} ({{ill|TT353|de|TT353|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/TT353|qq=}})—a day-accurate assignment was possible. In the tomb of Senenmut it is recorded that Seba-en-Sah culminated at [[Midnight]] on {{ill|23. Achet III|de|Achet#Datierungen|lt=23rd Achet III|lt_de=23. Achet III|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/23. Achet III|qq=}}. The constellations mentioned in Senenmut’s tomb, as in other ancient Egyptian sources, refer to the observational site of the calendrical Sothis risings, namely Memphis. {{ill|Rolf Krauss|de|Rolf Krauss|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Rolf Krauss|qq=}}, who postulated the hypothesis of changing observational sites ({{ill|Axiom|de|Axiom|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Axiom|qq=}}),, on the other hand, rejects an identification of Seba-en-Sah with {{ill|Rigel|de|Rigel|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Rigel|qq=}}, because in his published analyses {{ill|Elephantine|de|Elephantine|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Elephantine|qq=}} is favored as the observational site. Accepting the equation of Seba-en-Sah with Rigel would render his concept invalid. In the Ramesside Star Clocks, which were created only about three centuries later, the unchanged data from Senenmut’s tomb reappear, although in the {{ill|Egyptian calendar|de|altägyptischen Kalender|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Egyptian calendar|qq=}} the star positions had shifted by more than two months. Astronomical calculations showed that the midnight culmination of Seba-en-Sah in conjunction with the other stellar data can be reconciled with the ancient Egyptian calendar and the observational site Memphis only for the years 1463/1462 BCE. {| class="wikitable zebra" style="background:#FFFAF0; width: 98%; border: 2px solid gray; text-align: center;" |- {{Ägyptologie TblHighlight}} !colspan="4" style="background:#FFE39B"| Altägyptischer Kalender der Ramessidischen Sternuhren im Jahr 1463/1462 v.
